title: Palestrina
hookLine: the composer whose music showed Trent that many voices can serve the words

cards: A small choir stands in a stone chapel in Rome. One voice starts a line. A second comes in a moment later, singing the same tune a little higher.
Then a third, a fourth, until the room is full of separate lines weaving over and under each other; none of them is the melody, and all of them are. It sounds like one breath.
Bishops at a church council had worried that music like this buried the words of the Mass. At the center of the story people tell about it is a choirmaster from a hill town near Rome.
The town was called Palestrina, and so was he.

teach.b: Today's word is polyphony: many voices, each singing its own line at the same time. First, the worry.
At the Council of Trent, bishops complained that some church music had become showy, mixed with worldly songs, with so many voices tangled together that nobody could hear the prayer.

teach.h: THE LEGEND OF THE MASS THAT SAVED IT.
teach.b: The council's decree barred music that was lascivious or impure from the Mass, and some bishops pressed for words that could be clearly understood. Second, the legend.

A story grew up afterward: the council was ready to ban polyphony altogether, until Palestrina wrote a Mass so clear and beautiful that it changed their minds. That Mass carries the name of a pope, Marcellus.
Historians aren't sure it happened that way, but the story stuck because the music fits it. Third, the music.

teach.h: VOICES TAKE TURNS SO WORDS COME THROUGH.
teach.b: In Palestrina's writing the voices take turns, so the words come through, then blend again. Nothing shouts. No single singer is the star.
The Second Vatican Council gave Gregorian chant pride of place in the Roman liturgy, and said other kinds of sacred music, especially polyphony, are not excluded.
Choirs from cathedrals to small parishes still sing Palestrina at Mass.

teach.h: LET EVERY SPIRIT PRAISE THE LORD.
teach.b: Psalm one hundred fifty ends, in the Douay-Rheims: "Let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia." Every voice on its own line, and one prayer underneath them all.

how: Catholic cathedral and parish choirs sing Renaissance polyphony, including Palestrina's Masses and motets, at solemn Masses, alongside Gregorian chant.

games.q: you're a choirmaster in Rome. the bishops say church music has become a tangle and nobody can hear the words. what do you write?
o: louder, showier music, so people pay attention.
music where the voices take turns, so the words come through.
games.why: Palestrina's music lets the voices take turns and blend again, so the words come through. that's why the legend about him stuck.

practice: If you can, play a recording of his music quietly, maybe the Mass named for Pope Marcellus; with no recording, sit with the sounds around you and pick out one at a time.
Follow one voice, high or low, for a while, then let go and hear them all together. If you pray, let the music carry your prayer; if you don't, simply listen.

wordCard.voice: Polyphony. Many voices, each singing its own line at once, woven so the words of the prayer still come through.

orig.note: Latin: polyphony, the word Vatican II's constitution on the liturgy uses when it says this music is not excluded.

carryVoice: Your line: many voices, one word. Looking back: martyrs in Vietnam, hidden families in Japan, Mother Seton, John Carroll, the king of Kongo, a hard history, and Palestrina. Day eight hundred eighty-two, done.
